articles.title_orig: Iran’s precision strikes picked apart Gulf infrastructure, blunting US war plans
articles.title_zh: Iran’s precision strikes picked apart Gulf infrastructure, blunting US war plans
articles.content_orig:
Iran and its allies hit water plants, airports, refineries and a nuclear power station across the Persian Gulf with a precision that rules out the official story of falling debris, a Reuters investigation has found, showing the civilian damage was the aim, not a side effect.
Reuters counted at least 135 drone and missile strikes on at least 84 infrastructure sites in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain since the war began on February 28. Again and again, the munitions struck the one piece of equipment a facility could least afford to lose, some of it hidden under rooftops or only a few meters across.
Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, has said as much. “It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed,” he wrote on X in early September.
“American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure.” Three days later, three pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline were hit.
Reuters based its findings on 36 interviews, imagery and satellite data.
In at least 34 statements, the region’s governments blamed damage on debris from successful interceptions. Fourteen experts who reviewed Reuters’ imagery, 11 from the affected industries, said that was highly improbable, citing signs of explosive detonation and the importance of what was hit.
Five of the states make it illegal to photograph or share certain images of strike damage.
‘Running out of water in days’
Kuwait, a desert country, draws 90 percent of its drinking water from desalination plants, most of them attached to coastal power stations because removing salt from seawater takes enormous amounts of heat and electricity.
Iran hit at least four of Kuwait’s eight combined power and desalination plants between March 2 and July 20, Reuters found, some more than once. In one four-day period in July, it struck what the government called “several” desalination plants, one of them at least twice.
“If you were to attack enough of their capacity, we’re talking about running out of water in days or weeks,” said Michael Christopher Low, director of the Middle East Center at the University of Utah. Donald Trump had threatened Iran’s water supply in March, Low said, but it was Iran that turned the threat into reality for its neighbors.
Kuwait’s government asked citizens to save water and electricity in “the spirit of shared responsibility.”
The strikes also hit Kuwait’s main refineries. In April it exported no crude at all, the first time since 1991, according to TankerTrackers.
On May 17, a drone hit an electrical substation at the UAE’s Barakah nuclear plant, about 130 meters from a reactor, forcing one of its four reactors onto emergency diesel generators, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency.
“This means whoever was or is behind this knew exactly what they were doing,” IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said.
Three officials told Reuters Iran had the plant’s floor plan. The UAE said the drone came from “armed factions in Iraq.” There was no radioactive release.
The UAE’s main oil port outside the Strait of Hormuz, Fujairah was the region’s lifeline once Iran blockaded the strait. It was struck at least 19 times, and for the first three months of the war was either under attack or under repair.
The first strike, on March 3, left tanks burning that were still visible from space two days later. On March 9, a strike destroyed the first of the port’s two matrix manifolds, a junction of 62 pipelines that carries crude and refined products from the terminals to the ships. Emirati officials blamed debris.
“This is a wound to the brain and heart,” said Ramanan Krishnamoorti, a petroleum engineering professor at the University of Houston, who said it stretched credibility that debris had simply fallen onto the manifold.
Strikes on March 14, 16 and 17, beginning hours after a US attack on Iran’s Kharg Island oil terminal, damaged the second manifold, Reuters found, a hit not previously reported. Loadings fell to 440,000 barrels a day in the week of March 16, less than half the 2025 average, according to Kpler.
“We were watching it come in and watching the helicopters blast the drones out of the sky,” said a foreign businessman who watched one wave from a nearby road. “They were sending swarms of drones and one or two got through.” American-made Patriot batteries sat about 3 kilometers away.
The port recovered to a weekly record of 3.2 million barrels a day by the end of March. Iran struck again on April 6 and May 4, the second time hitting the pipes feeding the first manifold. Refined exports essentially stopped: a single ship left between May 4 and June 1, and they did not recover until September. In at least six statements, Emirati authorities blamed debris; none admitted major damage.
Strikes on UAE infrastructure stopped after May 17.
In June, four sources told Reuters, the UAE agreed to unlock at least $10 billion in frozen Iranian funds, $3 billion of which was released, and two said Iran agreed in return to stop attacking. The UAE denied any agreement. A senior Iranian official confirmed the transfer but said it reflected “the correction of the UAE’s behavior.”
In September, as Iran attacked ADNOC tankers at sea, Fujairah set a monthly export record of 2.62 million barrels a day.
At Qatar’s Ras Laffan, which handles nearly a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas, two strikes destroyed the cold boxes that chill gas into liquid. QatarEnergy says repairs will take three to five years.
On September 10, the attack on the East-West Pipeline halted crude flowing across the desert to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, a route for up to 4 percent of global supply. Riyadh blamed Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Iran-linked strikes have damaged five of Saudi Arabia’s nine biggest refineries and output fell from more than 10 million barrels a day to below 7 million, a loss of over $50 billion.
Airports in at least four countries, Amazon data centers and the UAE’s Al Taweelah aluminum smelter were also hit. The smelter will not return to normal before 2027.
“Every single target was civilian,” said Sultan Al Jaber, head of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. “They are targeting our infrastructure. But what they’re really targeting is our way of life.”
The Houthis and the Red Sea
After the April ceasefire collapsed, Revolutionary Guards commanders flew to Yemen on July 13 with missile and drone equipment for the Houthis, according to Reuters.
From July 16 to 18, US forces hit bridges and a tunnel on the roads to Bandar Abbas, strikes Iran International mapped in its investigation of Iran’s road and rail network.
The Houthis answered by hitting Saudi Arabia, knocking the Jazan refinery’s output to zero. The group has since declared a naval embargo on Saudi Red Sea ports, hit tankers and the airport in Najran, and taken the port of Mokha. On Saturday, a strike blamed on the Houthis killed 12 people at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia’s crown prince asked Trump for military help in September and was rebuffed. Riyadh had already signed a mutual defense pact in Mecca with Turkey and Pakistan in August.
In 1983, a CIA assessment warned that “even a few attacks against well-chosen targets could do considerable damage” to the region’s oil facilities. Fujairah, which began full operations the same year, has since been struck at least 19 times.
Iran has approximately 128,000 hectares of vineyards, just 31,000 fewer than Australia, whose wine exports were worth around €1.3 billion ($1.45 billion) in 2025.
The disparity reflects the disappearance of an industry from Iran's economy following the revolution, when the newly established Islamic Republic banned the production and sale of alcoholic beverages.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Senate GOP see Starlink become latest flash point over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump, Senate GOP see Starlink become latest flash point over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Scientists knew the Doomsday Glacier was melting. They didn’t realize how ‘aggressively’
articles.title_zh: Scientists knew the Doomsday Glacier was melting. They didn’t realize how ‘aggressively’
articles.content_orig:
The planet’s widest glacier is melting “more aggressively” than previously projected, meaning its impacts on global sea level rise could be double current estimates, according to new research by a team of glaciologists.
Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica — nicknamed the Doomsday Glacier because of the catastrophe its collapse would trigger — is a huge wildcard when it comes to forecasting global sea level rise.
Real-time coverage, so you're never caught off guard.
The Florida-sized glacier, which lies in one of the least accessible places on Earth, has been retreating for decades and its melting ice currently contributes around 4% to global sea level rise.
But the mechanisms behind its retreat are exceptionally complex, making it tricky to precisely map out its future.
It’s a vital task, however, as Thwaites holds enough water to raise sea levels by more than 2 feet if it were to collapse. Because it also acts as a cork holding back the vast Antarctic ice sheet, it could ultimately lead to around 10 feet of sea level rise, devastating coastal communities from Miami to Manila.
Glaciologists from the University of California, Irvine and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory have developed a new ice sheet model they say better reflects what’s happening underneath this ice giant.
Thwaites’ rapid retreat is driven by processes at its “grounding line” — the point at which the ice rises up from the seabed and starts to float on the ocean as an ice shelf.
But while typical ice sheet models have tended to view the grounding line as something fixed and mostly stable, “we have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth’s major ocean-terminating glaciers,” said the report’s lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA who was an Earth system science researcher at UC Irvine at the time of the study.
Satellite data reveals the grounding line is actually a “grounding zone,” sometimes miles wide, where seawater constantly flushes in and out with the tides, lifting and lowering the thick ice in a process known as “tidal pumping.” This allows relatively warm ocean water to penetrate “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” Poinelli said.
When the scientists adjusted models to include the concept of a grounding zone, they found Thwaites could contribute up to 1.2 inches of sea level rise by 2100 — twice previous estimates — even without further global warming, according to the findings published Monday in the journal Nature Communications.
Scientists looked deep beneath the Doomsday Glacier. What they found spells potential disaster for the planet
The land on which Thwaites sits slopes downward, meaning as the glacier melts, more ice is exposed to warm ocean water. The topography is complicated, however, by two key underwater ridges, which “pin” the ice, holding it back from flowing into the ocean more rapidly.
The melting processes at Thwaites’ grounding zone are accelerating the “unpinning” of ice from a large ridge called the Mouginot Ridge, the study found. There is a 60% chance that it will be unpinned by the end of the century, the study found, after which the glacier is likely to retreat quickly down the sloping bedrock toward the next major ridge.
The findings suggest the impacts of losing Thwaites might have been underestimated. A sea level rise of 1.2 inches may not sound much but it’s enough to greatly magnify dangers to coastal populations.
The results “predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades,” said Eric Rignot, a report author and professor of Earth system science at UC Irvine.
Ted Scambos, a senior research scientist for the Earth Science and Observation Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, who was not involved in the research, said the findings could be “a real gamechanger for sea level forecasting from Thwaites.”
But he and other experts caution that more research is needed to understand the impacts of different grounding zone melting processes, not least by getting direct data from underneath the glacier.
Journey to the disappearing edge of the Arctic
“The reality is that there is a lot we still need to find out about grounding zone processes to be able to make confident predictions about how fast ice will be lost,” said Robert Larter, a marine geophysicist at British Antarctic Survey, who was also not involved in the study. The environment beneath Thwaites, which is very difficult to access, is even more complex than the paper describes, he added.
Getting observational data from Thwaites’ grounding line is the next step, Rignot said. The scientists are planning to travel there in 2028 to deploy instruments able to document the flushing in and out of seawater.
“We have been aware of the impacts of climate change on our planet’s sensitive ice sheets for decades,” Rignot said, “but a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is really happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm.”
He said the world must cut planet-heating pollution now to limit the impacts but warned, “even if we do, we can expect higher sea levels in the future resulting from the damage that has already been done.”

articles.title_zh: Red Magic 12 Pro+ gaming phone launches with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, liquid-cooling system, 8,400mAh battery, and more
articles.content_orig:
Add GIZMOCHINA as Preferred Source on Google
As an Amazon Associate, Gizmochina earns from qualifying purchases. Links on this page may earn us a commission at no extra cost to you.
Red Magic 12 Pro+ has officially launched in China with a range of hardware upgrades aimed at mobile gamers. The new flagship combines high-refresh-rate visuals with advanced cooling technology and a large battery. It also retains several gaming-focused features, including a 3.5mm headphone jack and dedicated shoulder triggers. Here’s everything you need to know about Red Magic’s newest gaming phone.
Starting from the front, the Red Magic 12 Pro+ features a 6.85-inch BOE X11 OLED display with a 2,688 × 1,216-pixel resolution, a 185Hz refresh rate and ultra-narrow 0.96mm bezels. Since it does not have a camera punch-hole, it offers a truly full-screen viewing experience.
The panel supports a 500Hz touch sampling rate and up to 5,000Hz instantaneous touch sampling, alongside 10-bit colors, 1,900 nits of global brightness and 5,000 nits of local peak brightness. It also offers 2,592Hz PWM dimming at low brightness and DC-like dimming at higher brightness.
Performance comes from Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, paired with RedCore R5 gaming and G1 display control chips. The phone supports LPDDR5T memory running at up to 10,667Mbps and UFS 4.1 Pro storage. Red Magic also supports simultaneous super-resolution and frame interpolation at up to 2K resolution and 185Hz in compatible games.
The device packs an 8,400mAh battery with 120W wired charging, 80W wireless charging, and bypass charging for powering the phone directly during gaming. Its ICE cooling system combines an active cooling fan with a liquid-cooling setup, alongside additional thermal materials. The built-in fan reaches 25,500rpm and carries an IPX8 water-resistance rating, while the phone itself is rated IP68 and IP69 for dust and water resistance.
The rear camera setup comprises a 50-megapixel primary camera with optical image stabilization and a 50-megapixel ultra-wide camera. A 16-megapixel OmniVision sensor sits beneath the display for selfies and video calls.
The phone runs Android 17-based RedMagic OS 12 and features an ultrasonic in-screen fingerprint sensor. Other features include 700Hz shoulder triggers, dual 1115E linear speakers, three microphones, an X-axis linear motor, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.3, NFC, an IR blaster, USB 3.2 Gen 2 and a 3.5mm headphone jack.
In China, the Red Magic 12 Pro+ is available in Dark Night Transparent, Silver Wing Transparent and Ice Blue Transparent finishes. The 12GB+256GB model is priced at 6,999 Yuan (~$1,050), while the 16GB+512GB and 16GB+1TB variants cost 7,999 Yuan (~$1,200) and 8,999 Yuan (~$1,350), respectively.
Red Magic also previewed a limited-edition Golden Saga model with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, featuring a forged-carbon cooling design. Its price and exact release date have yet to be announced. There is no confirmed international availability yet.
What’s your opinion about the Red Magic 12 Pro+ gaming phone’s specs and price? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: China indicates rare earths will keep flowing to EU, regardless of U.S. trade deal expiration
articles.title_zh: China indicates rare earths will keep flowing to EU, regardless of U.S. trade deal expiration
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — China intends to keep exporting rare earths to Europe regardless of whether a U.S. trade deal with Beijing gets extended past January.
The world's second-largest economy is willing to continue approving rare earth licenses to Europe, China's Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong told CNBC when asked on Thursday about the impact of the upcoming U.S. deadline.
Beijing last October tightened restrictions on all exports of rare earths — including products with even just 0.1% of China-sourced rare earths . The move followed a new U.S. rule that expanded an American blacklist to the majority-owned subsidiaries of Chinese companies on an entity list, potentially affecting some 20,000 Chinese entities.
However, both the U.S. and China agreed to suspend those measures for one year at a meeting in late October 2025 between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump. Ahead of the leaders' latest summit last month, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the truce was extended by two months to January.
Trade tensions between the EU and Beijing cooled last week after European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič met with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing . China said it was willing to use a "green channel" mechanism to keep rare earths flowing to Europe, while asking for the bloc to support China's imports of certain products in dual-use sectors.
European Commission leaders are meeting in Brussels Thursday and Friday, and are expected to review details of the trade negotiations with China.

The Dutch firm expects China to account for 20 per cent of its total sales this year, even as the US pushes for tighter export restrictions
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year, after seeing shipments to the market more than double during the previous quarter despite mounting US pressure for tighter export restrictions on less advanced chipmaking machinery.
The company’s sales to China surged 109 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, according to financial results released on Wednesday. That took China’s share of ASML’s machine sales to 23 per cent, up from 14 per cent in the second quarter.
The revenue jump comes as Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten faces pressure from Washington to tighten restrictions on sales of chipmaking machines to China.

articles.title_orig: The world’s most dangerous tree lives in Florida. Here’s how it can kill you
articles.title_zh: The world’s most dangerous tree lives in Florida. Here’s how it can kill you
articles.content_orig:
Anthony Talcott , Digital Journalist
ORLANDO, Fla. – Florida is no stranger to danger, whether it’s massive sinkholes , powerful hurricanes , or invasive threats .
But what many residents might not know is that there’s a tree native to the Sunshine State that’s considered the most dangerous in the world.
That’s according to the Guinness World Records , which has granted the moniker to the Manchineel tree.
At first glance, there doesn’t appear to be anything all that dangerous about the Manchineel.
The tree is native to South Florida, and it gets its name from the Spanish word for “little apple,” which references the fruit that can be seen growing on the Manchineel.
However, researchers with the UF/IFAS warn that the tree has also been dubbed the “Tree of Death” due to the plant’s and its fruit’s deadly nature.
According to the UF/IFAS, all parts of the Manchineel tree are extremely poisonous, as the tree oozes a sap from its leaves, twigs, bark and fruit that can cause burn-like blisters when it comes into contact with skin.
“People have reported heavy inflammation of the eyes and even temporary blindness from irritants carried in the smoke of this tree’s burning wood,” researchers wrote. “While some claim that they are immune to the noxious sap when it interacts with their skin, ingesting any part of this tree can be lethal and is not recommended.”
[BELOW: Invasive chameleons infest Central Florida neighborhood]
Over two decades ago , a doctor who inadvertently tasted the Manchineel’s fruit described it as “pleasantly sweet,” though she later noticed a “strange peppery feeling” in her mouth.
Soon, that feeling coalesced into a burning sensation and tightness in her throat. The symptoms reportedly became excruciating and took around eight hours to subside.
“Even standing under this tree in the rain can be harmful,” another study states . “Reports of students who took shelter during a storm under this tree gave rise to concurrent dermatitis and ophthalmitis .”
The sap’s poison is so potent, researchers claim, that Native Americans historically used the substance to coat their arrows when hunting.
Nowadays, warning signs and red rings are often posted near Manchineels to warn unwary visitors to stay away.
That being said, most residents in the state aren’t likely to come across a Manchineel during their day-to-day routine.
This is because the Manchineel tree is an endangered species, meaning it’s in danger of becoming extinct.
[BELOW: Here’s the story behind the ‘Devil’s Tree’ in Florida]
In the Sunshine State, the tree can be primarily found in the Everglades, with reports documented in Monroe and Miami-Dade counties.
Regardless, though, it’s a good idea to give a wide berth to any of these trees if you come across one. After all, coming into contact with its sap in any way could put you in an incredibly painful situation — or worse.

articles.title_orig: Still smiling at 117, Albanian may be world's oldest woman
articles.title_zh: Still smiling at 117, Albanian may be world's oldest woman
articles.content_orig:
At 117, Qamile Marra is not particularly concerned with proving she may be the world's oldest woman -- or even persuading Albanian pension officials that she is not dead.
For a woman born under Ottoman rule, who turned 36 a fortnight before the end of World War II and outlived Albania's communist dictatorship, her focus remains firmly on enjoying life.
"Life is beautiful, like Mount Tomorr in bloom," she told AFP with a smile, referring to one of Albania's loftiest peaks as she sat outside her home in Ferras, about 100 kilometres (60 miles) south of the capital.
Surrounded by fruit trees, Marra has spent almost her entire life in the village, growing her own food and tending livestock.
"You live as long as God has decreed," she said, her deeply wrinkled face framed by a traditional white headscarf.
According to her birthdate as listed on several official documents -- August 19, 1909 -- Marra would be two days older than Britain's Ethel Caterham, recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's oldest living woman.
Definitively proving the age of "supercentenarians" can be difficult.
Many of the people famous for living the longest are from places where shoddy recordkeeping and suspected pension fraud are rampant, according to a study that won the 2024 Ig Nobel prize, which awards offbeat scientific research.
But Marra has extensive records that appear to confirm her age.
Her relatives have contacted Guinness and hold a birth certificate issued in 1945, a passport issued in 1978 and a recent identity card, all showing the same date of birth.
Her age even surprised local authorities, who stopped her pension when she turned 100, according to her 80-year-old son Hysen.
"They didn't believe my mother was still alive," he said, recalling how he had to show proof, including witness statements, to resume the meagre payments.
Earlier this month, the government issued her a special state pension to mark her age.
Perhaps the answer lies in Marra's habits and lifestyle.
She rises early to sweep the yard, water her flowers and feed the chickens before settling down with her favourite coffee.
She still enjoys regular walks through her carefully tended orchard with her son, who lives with her, stopping to pick ripe pomegranates along the way.
She also slips basil leaves in her pockets to "enjoy the aroma".
Whatever the secret, her son says she has never even visited a doctor.
"She is in good health and has never taken any medication."
Marra's husband died 36 years ago, but she still smiles when talking about their decades together -- an arranged marriage, but a loving one.
"Otherwise, how could I have had seven children with him?" she said.
She has now seen five generations of her family grow up around her.
Tears welled up as she remembered the family and friends she had lost. But her face brightened when a niece called to chat.
"I've watched them get engaged, marry and build their own homes and lives," she said.
"When I see people coming and going in the house, I am so happy."
From her own youth, she has kept a single photograph: a near-century-old picture of a young woman wearing a white scarf just like the one she had on.

articles.title_orig: UNESCO hosted regional capacity-building workshop for natural World Heritage in Central Asia and Mongolia in Almaty - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.title_zh: UNESCO hosted regional capacity-building workshop for natural World Heritage in Central Asia and Mongolia in Almaty - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.source: International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.content_orig:
UNESCO and IUCN brought together State Party representatives and site managers from the heart of Eurasia, with support of the UNESCO/Republic of Korea Funds-in-Trust project aiming to enhance transnational cooperation.
13 October 2026 -  The capacity-building workshop for natural World Heritage properties in Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan) and Mongolia was held in Almaty on 7 and 8 October 2026. The two-day event aimed to further strengthen the technical capacity of site managers and national authorities to protect natural World Heritage properties, with a particular focus on transboundary cooperation.
The workshop was coordinated by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre , the UNESCO Regional Offices in Almaty and Beijing and IUCN . It was built on the 2025 capacity-building workshop held under the same project, which aims to enhance transboundary cooperation among natural and mixed World Heritage properties in Asia by strengthening existing site management, mapping knowledge and capacity gaps, and identifying further opportunities for transboundary cooperation.
The workshop was financed by the Republic of Korea through the UNESCO/Republic of Korea Funds-in-Trust project “Enhancing Transnational Cooperation and Fostering Peace: Natural and Mixed World Heritage in Asia”. The project’s donor is the Korea Heritage Service (KHS). Russian–English interpretation was provided throughout.
Participants reviewed the concept of Outstanding Universal Value and World Heritage activities in Central Asia and Mongolia, including state of conservation, Periodic Reporting, the Upstream Process, Preliminary Assessments and nominations. They discussed how to ensure management effectiveness using tools such as Enhancing our Heritage Toolkit (EoH) 2.0 and the new 2026 Managing World Heritage Manual, and how conservation principles and governance help sustain the values and integrity of properties. State Party representatives and site managers shared experiences from Tajik National Park (Mountains of the Pamirs) , the Tugay forests of the Tigrovaya Balka Nature Reserve (Tajikistan), Western Tien-Shan (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan), Cold Winter Deserts of Turan (Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan), Uvs Nuur Basin (Mongolia/Russian Federation) and Landscapes of Dauria (Mongolia/Russian Federation), followed by lively exchanges among the participants. Scientific research and monitoring were also on the agenda, including species as indicators of ecosystem health, monitoring needs, techniques and tools, and common challenges, alongside the IKI project “One Health in Nature Conservation in Central Asia” and its support for World Heritage properties.
Natural heritage knows no borders; its conservation requires our shared responsibility and collective commitment. Central Asia and Mongolia are home to invaluable Outstanding Universal Value and unique ecosystems. - Ms Yunjung Lee, Director, World Heritage Division, Korea Heritage Service
The main tools for tackling issues are coordination, capacity building and awareness raising. These require a change in attitudes and in management approaches in our daily work.  And for this we need to establish cooperation and improve existing coordination. - Mr Amir Piric, Director, UNESCO Regional Office in Almaty
A significant part of the discussion focused on transboundary conservation and management. Participants examined conservation principles and governance through case studies of the serial transnational World Heritage properties represented at the workshop, as well as other examples from Asia such as Phong Nha-Ke Bang and Hin Nam No National Parks (Lao PDR/Viet Nam). Lessons learned from the East Asian–Australasian Flyway Partnership (EAAFP) highlighted the importance of connecting people, including site managers, and building relationship and trust as the foundation of regional cooperation and conservation across borders.
Experts from ICCROM and IUCN addressed how to assess impacts on Outstanding Universal Value, including Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs), assessing cumulative impacts through Strategic Environmental Assessments (SEAs) and the transboundary dimensions of regional impact assessments. The new GEF8 EcoLand joint IUCN-UNDP project on “Integrated Conservation Management and Restoration of High-Value Landscapes in Uzbekistan” was presented, together with opportunities through UNESCO’s Natural Sciences programmes and the outcomes of UNCCD COP17 in Mongolia. An interactive exercise mapped networks and potential synergies, and the workshop concluded with reflections, feedback and a discussion of strategic next steps.
Representatives of each State Party shared their reflections on the workshop and highlighted potential follow-up activities, including strengthening operational capacities (e.g. harmonization of Tentative Lists, SEAs and resource mobilization) and further exploring thematic areas such as sustainable tourism, invasive species and climate change, through knowledge-sharing and exchange, as well as the development of a common communication platform. Building on the rich discussions during the workshop and with the support of the UNESCO/Republic of Korea Funds-in-Trust project, UNESCO and IUCN will continue to engage with national authorities and site managers across the region to support their ongoing efforts to safeguard the natural heritage located in the heart of Eurasia and further strengthen transnational cooperation.
Conservation funding rarely reaches the people who know the lands and territories best. Podong sets…
Government and scientific and technical experts from across sectors started jointly identifying how…
IUCN, through the Oceania Regional Office, is pleased to welcome Te Tira Whakamātaki from Aotearoa…

articles.title_orig: IMF-World Bank meetings draw modest protests in Bangkok over growing inequality
articles.title_zh: IMF-World Bank meetings draw modest protests in Bangkok over growing inequality
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK (AP) — Dozens of people marched in Bangkok on Thursday, seeking to draw the attention of world financial leaders to poverty, pollution and other grievances during a meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
Protesters, some wearing masks of U.S. President Donald Trump, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva and other leaders, dragged a float of a big pink pig with dollar signs for eyes toward the venue, briefly blocking traffic near the rigorously guarded convention center where more than 15,000 officials and experts were gathered for the IMF’s autumn meeting.
The protesters were also demonstrating against financial institutions and against what they said were the “vile abuses” of the Thai government and financial institutions.
“Our country is facing a crisis of household debt. Our people are growing poorer. Our environment is deteriorating. Climate disasters are intensifying,” the People’s Network Against the World Bank and IMF said in a written declaration.
Thailand has used the meetings as an opportunity to showcase its capital city, where luxury hotels and other trappings of extreme wealth contrast with shantytowns, fetid canals and people sleeping rough along major thoroughfares.
Recent severe floods have wrecked crops and damaged millions of homes and businesses, adding to the hardships for many Thais.
Apart from a minor scuffle with police on a pedestrian bridge, the peaceful protesters marched from the nearby Khlong Toei slum toward the convention center and then disbanded.
Growing inequality and the challenges posed by climate-related disasters and war are among the many problems leaders are discussing during their weeklong meetings.
Thailand is among many low- and middle-income countries, especially net energy importers, that have struggled as the Iran war has pushed oil prices past $100 a barrel for much of this year. It also is the most income-unequal country in the region, according to the World Bank.
In its latest forecasts, the IMF has warned that rising prices and debt are worsening inequality in many of its 191 member economies.
In Asia, regional economic growth is projected to slow to 4.8% this year from 5% in 2025, and then to 4.4% in 2027, dragged lower by the back-to-back shocks of the pandemic, the Ukraine war, the Iran war and higher tariffs and other trade barriers, IMF economists say.
The IMF chief and other top economic experts have emphasized the need for countries, including Thailand, to ensure they control debt by focusing their government spending on helping their most vulnerable people with targeted and temporary assistance.
Associated Press journalists Haruka Nuga and Sakchai Lalit contributed to this report.
_src_links: IMF-World Bank meetings draw modest protests in Bangkok over growing inequality

articles.title_orig: Why Does Saudi Arabia Struggle to Stop Houthi Attacks?
articles.title_zh: Why Does Saudi Arabia Struggle to Stop Houthi Attacks?
articles.content_orig:
The attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia have pushed the war in Yemen to a new level. The targeting of civilian infrastructure, including airports, which has killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds, has left no room to maintain the “red lines” that previously outlined the limits of escalation.
This is a reckless gamble by the Houthis which is not in their interest. They are aware that the retaliation will be fierce, yet they continue to attack Saudi Arabia to fulfil Iran’s agenda that seeks heightened tensions before the United States midterms.
Given the motivation to escalate, the present situation has the potential to develop into two scenarios: A major region-wide operation against the Houthis or a war of attrition.
In response to the Houthi escalation, Saudi Arabia is striving to garner maximum international support while deepening its regional and international alliances. The aim is to come up with a united front capable of taking on what has become a regional threat.
Riyadh is certainly looking to its Gulf neighbours who, themselves, are impacted by the continuing conflict in the region. There is a collective realisation that everyone is in grave danger, not just Saudi Arabia.
Therefore, Gulf states – perhaps with the exception of Oman – will support Riyadh both directly and indirectly in the fighting in Yemen.
Pakistan and Turkiye are also likely to join the front, having signed with Saudi Arabia a defence agreement known as the Mecca Pact. The pact is to be ratified by the Turkish parliament in the next few days, opening the way for Turkish military deployment in support of Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, indirect involvement by Turkiye and Pakistan, along with logistical and intelligence support, appears to be already well under way.
A US intervention is also possible, although it seems unlikely before the US midterms, as military engagements in the Middle East remain unpopular among US voters.
A region-wide coalition can help support the counteroffensive of the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government already under way. This could give the necessary push to retake the western coastal region, including areas beyond Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab.
Such gains could ease pressure on Red Sea shipping and potentially shift the military balance in favour of the government. The opening of additional fronts across other Yemeni cities and governorates could stretch Houthi forces, disperse their resources, and increase the likelihood of further government advances.
Retaking Sanaa could also be on the horizon. The primary obstacle delaying the Yemeni government’s recapture of the city is internal discord among the various factions within the government itself, compounded by negative external interference that exacerbates these rifts and weakens the collective effort to confront the Houthis.
Recent measures taken by the government, specifically efforts to unify its decision-making and consolidate its military operations command, have yielded noticeable progress on the ground. However, achieving the ultimate objective of retaking Sanaa requires sustained effort and focused determination.
If government forces make substantial gains, that could force the Houthis to offer concessions in exchange for a pause in fighting. They have done that before. Their purpose would not be to seek peace but to get enough breathing room to regroup and eventually go back to fighting. Negotiators should keep that in mind when approaching talks with the Houthis.
If the Saudi-led coalition and the Yemeni government succumb to internal divisions and disagreements, this may slow progress against the Houthis. This would allow the Houthi fighters to hold on to their positions while increasing their pressure on the strategic town of Taiz and maintaining the campaign against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia.
Such a development could further complicate the conflict, increase civilian casualties and displacement, and prolong the war without producing a decisive military outcome.
This will have a significant economic impact on Saudi Arabia and complicate the implementation of its development goals, as it would have to prioritise defence spending.
The rest of the Gulf economies will also be negatively impacted because Saudi Arabia plays such a central role in the region. What is more, losing ground to the Houthis would mean that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would also continue, disrupting energy exports from the region.
In this scenario, there will be “no victor, no vanquished” deadlock in Yemen, but Iran would emerge as winner. A war of attrition along the Red Sea coast would provide Tehran with significant breathing room, allowing it to alleviate pressure on its own war efforts.
This would enable Iran to use the Houthi card as leverage in the intermittent negotiations it conducts with the international community, emboldening it to raise the bar regarding its conditions and demands during those talks.
This means that the only way to resolve the crisis in Yemen is decisive military action led by the Yemeni government and supported by a region-wide coalition. For that to happen, the government has to get its internal affairs and its relations with allies in order.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title_orig: Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
articles.title_zh: Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
articles.content_orig:
The world’s timekeepers are meeting on Thursday near Paris to decide whether to scrap the “leap second”, which could disconnect the clocks we use from the Earth’s rotation and realign timescales.
The world’s clocks are designed on the idea that the Earth completes one rotation on its axis in exactly 24 hours. But it actually wobbles, making the time the Earth takes to rotate less exact. And over time, the Earth’s rotation is gradually slowing.
To compensate for that, since 1972, timekeepers have added a leap second every few years – the last one was added in 2016 – to keep clocks and Earth’s rotation in synchronisation.
But pressure has been mounting to scrap the leap second since it complicates matters for financial markets and data centres, which rely on precise timing down to milliseconds.
So what is a leap second? Could it be scrapped? And how might it change our understanding of time?
Clocks work based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the global standard that has been based on high-precision atomic clocks for more than seven decades. Atomic clocks mark time by observing the vibration of atoms.
But the Earth’s rotation works independently of atomic clocks.
A leap second is a second added periodically to UTC to make it synchronise with the Earth’s rotation. The first leap second was added to world clocks in 1972.
There have been 27 leap seconds added so far with the previous leap second being added on December 31, 2016. No further leap seconds have been added since.
According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), a nonregulatory federal agency of the United States Department of Commerce, leap seconds occur at the end of December or the end of June. The NIST also cites differences between the precision of the atomic second and the Earth’s rotation to explain the need for a leap second.
“The speed of the Earth’s rotation is not constant. …. This gradual decrease in the rotational rate is causing the duration of the mean solar second to gradually increase with respect to the atomic second,” the NIST added.
While leap seconds close the discrepancy between the Earth’s rotation and UTC, their addition has posed challenges for technology companies, financial markets and other businesses that depend on precise timings.
In 2012, LinkedIn and Reddit crashed after the addition of a leap second. The same year, ticket bookings for Qantas, the Australian airline, collapsed after the leap second was added.
Three years later, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission also issued a warning against it. And in July 2022, engineers at Meta said : “Every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures.”
With pressure mounting, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which has the French acronym BIPM, voted in 2022 to scrap the leap second by 2035. But countries like Russia have wanted to push the implementation date back to 2040. Russia incorporates leap seconds directly into its GLONASS satellite-navigation system, so delaying the scrapping of leap seconds would buy Russia time to update its satellite systems.
Despite Moscow’s concern, the 69 member states of BIPM are now meeting on Thursday in Versailles outside Paris to debate and vote on a resolution to scrap the leap second by 2027.
According to the BIPM, the timekeeping authorities of countries around the world will discuss three proposals at Versailles.
First, they will consider whether atomic clocks are still the most accurate device when it comes to measuring what constitutes a second. Optical frequencies are now in fact more precise than atomic clocks. If a proposal to change how time is measured is accepted, the second might have a new definition, characterised by optical frequencies rather than the vibrations of atoms.
The second, most significant proposal pertains to dumping the leap second.
And finally, the third proposal on the table is a pitch to synchronise time measurements on Earth with a new time standard that NASA is developing for the moon.
Proposals that are accepted are expected to come into effect from May 20, 2027, World Metrology Day.
If the leap second is scrapped, then it means our clocks will no longer be tied to the Earth’s rotation.
According to the NIST, if this happens, “then adjustments would have to be made to time stamps and legacy equipment and software which synchronise to UTC for astronomical observations.”
“Some proposals have been made to implement larger corrections like leap hours, which would occur much less often than leap seconds,” it added.
Scientists said human routines will not be impacted and software glitches, data server crashes and network failures for financial markets will be eliminated with the abandonment of leap seconds.
But over a period of centuries, the gap between the Earth’s cycle and our clocks will become more apparent: By 2100, clocks will be ahead of the Earth by 54 seconds. In another two millennia, that gap would have widened to several hours. The result? Sunrise and sunset times that would feel out of sync with people’s natural rhythms today.

articles.title_orig: China’s Military Expansion in Southeast Asia Masks a More Complicated Reality
articles.title_zh: China’s Military Expansion in Southeast Asia Masks a More Complicated Reality
articles.content_orig:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
The Chinese Ministry of Defense’s announcement of a “joint support and training center” at an airport in Ban Keun, Laos, on Sept. 29 drew attention to the People’s Liberation Army’s growing footprint in Southeast Asia. Although China does not call it a “base” and said it’s “not targeted at any third party,” it is China’s first publicly acknowledged overseas military facility centered on airpower. Ban Keun joins Djibouti and Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base as nodes in a burgeoning network of overseas Chinese security infrastructure.
Concern is understandable. While smaller than China’s base in Djibouti, satellite imagery reveals eight light attack aircraft and support vehicles on a 2,000-meter runway that is currently under construction. Although insufficient to support long-range bombers, the facility likely benefits China’s logistics and intelligence capabilities, diversifies Southeast Asian base access beyond Cambodia, and ties Laos into its arms sales network. The joint center could eventually enhance the People’s Liberation Army Air Force’s power projection across mainland Southeast Asia, potentially affecting U.S. forces operating in the eastern Indian Ocean. For Vietnam , this development deepens its sense of siege .
The reflex among many policymakers in Washington after each rumored or announced Chinese military facility overseas is to interpret it through the lens of U.S.-Chinese competition. In Cambodia’s case with Ream, Washington imposed sanctions as punishment. Yet, this reflex misunderstands the nuanced interests driving regional partners to work with China — and how to counter it.
While the aviation facility in Laos demonstrates Beijing’s growing security presence in Southeast Asia, alignment is driven by diverse threat perceptions, notably regime security and intra-ASEAN concerns, rather than U.S.-China Cold War dynamics. Regional governments continue to hedge, leaving an opening for the United States to compete effectively with Beijing.
Compared to U.S. regional security engagement, China’s presence is less extensive but growing. China continues to militarize South China Sea land features. In mainland Southeast Asia, the Laos airfield joins the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, which opened in 2025 — officially under Cambodian control — and houses a rotating naval deployment . Cambodia , Laos, and Thailand stand out for the depth of military-to-military relationships with Beijing, while Indonesia , Malaysia and Thailand have recently established 2+2 dialogues with China, involving foreign and defense ministers from both countries. Arms sales are also a growth area for Beijing . Indonesia expects the delivery of J-10 fighter jets , while Beijing surpassed the United States as Bangkok’s primary supplier.
However, China’s strongest comparative advantage over the United States is its regime security provision. The Global Security Initiative, one of four foreign policy cooperation frameworks promoted by Beijing, promises internal security assistance to its authoritarian partners, boosting state capacity while advancing its preferred governance norms. Cambodia , Laos , Myanmar’s junta , and Vietnam have all formally signed on. Although Bangkok remains outside the framework, internal security and police cooperation (particularly targeting scam centers in Myanmar ) mirror the Thai military’s warm relations with the People’s Liberation Army.
Given the Chinese Communist Party’s holistic security conception equating party rule with national security, internal security arrangements often bleed over into external military cooperation. Notably, Beijing upgraded its 2+2 security dialogues with Cambodia , Laos , and Vietnam to 3+3 in 2026 by including the internal security ministries. For each of these regimes, China’s internal security provision is critical, as Beijing can export its substantial know-how in high-tech surveillance and paramilitary policing . In Vietnam’s case, the internal security cooperation addresses some of the paradox in its approach to China: despite threatening Vietnam’s South China Sea claims, China likely won’t overthrow the Communist Party of Vietnam, but a revolution could.
Viewed through the lens of U.S.-Chinese competition, one could assume that China’s growing security presence in Southeast Asia comes at Washington’s expense. The United States is distracted and underinvested in Southeast Asia, and China’s deepening security ties augment its unassailable economic predominance . Singaporean think tank ISEAS’ annual survey of ASEAN elites found in 2026 that a majority would side with Beijing if forced to make a choice in alignment.
Yet, the geopolitical landscape in Southeast Asia remains in flux, and alignments are multifaceted and ultimately transitory due to the region’s complex web of threat perceptions, including vis-à-vis China.  Indeed, ISEAS’ 2025 survey found that a majority would side with the United States — perhaps due to renewed South China Sea tensions. In 2024 , China led at 50.5 percent after a U.S. lead in prior years , likely as a result of U.S. support for Israel . Rather than representing durable shifts in regional alignment, the survey instead reflects in-the-moment reactions to specific events. Indeed, diving into other areas of the survey, such as which geopolitical events rank as top concerns for ASEAN governments, one finds little consensus on the perceived threats that drive alignment.
The region’s diverse and shifting threat perceptions, not great-power competition, do more to explain the incentives to forge closer security ties to China. Despite the bloc’s self-proclaimed role in reducing state-to-state conflict since the Cold War, some ASEAN states fear each other more than China or the United States, while also seeing Beijing as a friend in some respects (internal security) and a foe in others (maritime disputes). Southeast Asian governments do not evaluate China and the United States solely through the lens of great-power competition. Instead, their behavior reflects shifting calculations of external threat, internal regime security, and intraregional rivalries.
Landlocked Laos, as a fellow communist government, seems a natural partner for China, as it does not see Beijing as a direct security threat. Air force training and support boost Laos’ own capabilities, while ensuring Chinese economic assistance, despite the clear risks of dependence . If it can position itself as China’s preferred client, then it stands to benefit.
Although often derided in Washington as a “ Chinese puppet state ,” Cambodia’s regional security environment is more dangerous than Laos’. In addition to regime security considerations , part of the strategic calculus driving outreach to Beijing is to hedge against the potential security threats from its neighbors, Vietnam and Thailand. In 2025, disputes over land along their border sparked a short but sharp armed conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, which ended in a fragile ceasefire . Still-simmering Thai-Cambodian tensions underscore the risk of renewed war, incentivizing Phnom Penh to hope that security ties to China can offset relative weakness vis-à-vis its historic rivals or, at the very least, keep Beijing engaged as a friendly mediator.
This impulse — along with distrust of complete dependence upon Beijing — has spurred Phnom Penh to renew ties with the United States under the Trump administration, which is less concerned about human rights than past U.S. presidencies. After a 10-year hiatus, Washington and Phnom Penh plan to relaunch joint military exercises in 2027. Cambodia welcomed a U.S. Navy visit to Ream Naval Base earlier this year, presenting the base as under its control, not China’s. Simultaneously, Cambodia continues to pursue security ties with other powers, notably Japan .

articles.title_orig: Korea Stocks Tumble 8% as Investors Rush to Unwind AI Exposure
articles.title_zh: Korea Stocks Tumble 8% as Investors Rush to Unwind AI Exposure
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia , Micron and AMD were all down in premarket trading on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued a plummet that's seen over $1 trillion wiped from their market caps this week.
Nvidia fell 1.8%, Micron 4.4%, AMD 3.5%. Neoclouds also dropped, with CoreWeave down 5.3% and Nebius 4%. Oracle was trading at 2% lower.
20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment.
A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday.
South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%.
In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC , the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%.
Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML was last down 6.6%, Infineon Technologies shed 9.4%, and ASM International was down 9.6%, and Nokia fell 5%.
The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.
Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment.
China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028."
Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity.
The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.
Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust.
"Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note.
The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs.
"What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.

articles.title_orig: China launches 10 satellites aboard Zhuque-2E rocket to advance space-based AI computing
articles.title_zh: China launches 10 satellites aboard Zhuque-2E rocket to advance space-based AI computing
articles.content_orig:
China successfully launched 10 satellites aboard a Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket Wednesday, including eight designed to advance artificial intelligence computing capabilities in orbit.
The rocket lifted off at 7.40 pm local time (1140GMT) from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwestern China, placing all 10 satellites into their designated orbits, according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.
Eight satellites belong to the second group of the "Star Compute" project, developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company ADAspace.
Designed to operate in dawn-dusk orbits, the satellites carry high-performance computing systems, laser communication equipment, and low-light cameras.
They will test advanced technologies, including 10,000-watt liquid-cooling systems, large deployable cooling structures, space-based laser communication networks, and the training of AI foundation models directly in orbit.
ADAspace said the mission would help accelerate technological development and commercial applications of space-based computing.
The company plans to establish an orbital AI infrastructure network comprising 2,800 computing satellites.
The first group of 12 satellites was launched in May 2025. In January, the company announced it had deployed Alibaba's Qwen3 AI model aboard its orbital computing network, enabling AI processing directly in space.
The company aims to establish a 1,000-satellite network by 2030 and complete the larger constellation by 2035.

articles.title_orig: Exhibit focuses on World War II
articles.title_zh: Exhibit focuses on World War II
articles.content_orig:
Men from many areas of the United States were members of the 104th "Timberwolf" Division, which took a vital role in World War II. Elmer A. Anderson of Wildrose was among the infantry division's members.
An exhibit in the Dakota Territory Air Museum in Minot shows various items that belonged to Anderson, who enlisted in the U.S. Army following the U.S. entry into World War II. Some of the items were brought back to the U.S. after Anderson was overseas.
According to history compiled for the exhibit, Anderson, who was born in 1913 in Wildrose, served with the 104th, which saw combat in France, Belgium, Holland and Germany. The division was responsible for liberating the concentration camp at Nordhausen, Germany, in April 1945.
The items displayed were donated to the museum by Anderson’s family.
In the exhibit are an U.S. Army "Ike" jacket owned by Tech. Sgt. Anderson, Anderson's dog tags, a Faithful Service Medal, an enlisted man insignia, a marching compass and other items.
Jenna Grindberg, museum director, created the Anderson exhibit and other new exhibits with artifacts and stories not previously displayed until the 2026 season.
The museum's final day of the 2026 season is Sunday, Oct. 18. Visits are by appointment during the off season. This winter the museum is offering fully-guided World War II History Tours featuring the warplanes at the museum. The tours will be held during November-January. Those interested can contact the museum at 852-8500.

articles.title_orig: Stanford Student Union Includes Taiwan as Part of China
articles.title_zh: Stanford Student Union Includes Taiwan as Part of China
articles.content_orig:
The Associated Students of Stanford University (ASSU) posted an instagram picture that included Taiwan (ROC) as part of China (PRC). Last Friday, October 9th, ASSU posted profiles of the Undergraduate Senate for this academic year, including in their bios where each member was from and including an image of their state/country. For one senator who was from Shanghai, the image was of China, unmistakably including Taiwan.
The U.S. Congress has passed legislation (such as amendments in defense and spending bills championed by Representative Tom Tiffany) that legally bans the Pentagon, the State Department, and related federal agencies from using maps that depict Taiwan, Kinmen, Matsu, Penghu, and other islands as part of the People’s Republic of China (PRC).
The ASSU post came just two days after the former President of Taiwan, Tsai Ing-wen, delivered an address on US-Taiwan relations at the Hoover Institution, and one day after she gave the keynote at the annual Stanford DEFCON conference. Her talk focused on “sustained” pressure from China. This week, Taiwan stated that they are closely monitoring another series of live-fire drills conducted by China.
While Taiwan is not formally acknowledged by the United States as a sovereign state, the two countries hold critical unofficial ties. The Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 requires the United States to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, and just last year, the US removed a line from the State Department website which read, “we do not support Taiwan independence,” prompting anger from the Chinese state.
Aside from legal obligations, Taiwan is a major strategic player in the global economy, and particularly in the AI race between China and the US. Taiwan holds a near monopoly on the underlying AI tech stack, manufacturing 90% of semiconductor chips and the advanced packaging necessary for such systems. As a WSJ opinion piece put it, “Taiwan’s autonomy is a prerequisite for U.S. AI dominance.”
The Review has reached out to ASSU to determine whether the image was intentional or an accidental oversight. The move comes at a uniquely fraught time in discussions over Taiwanese sovereignty. ASSU is Stanford’s sole undergraduate legislative body, and represents the over seven thousand undergraduates on its campus. ASSU ought to be aware that they represent not just the student body, but but Stanford University itself.

articles.title_orig: YouTube couple drive 66,000 miles around world in campervan
articles.title_zh: YouTube couple drive 66,000 miles around world in campervan
articles.content_orig:
A couple who found YouTube fame with their travels around the world in a camper van are part-way into their next big adventure.
Chris and Marianne Fisher from Shropshire visited 29 countries and travelled 66,000 miles in their last great journey, receiving 27 million views on their Tread the Globe channel.
After returning home in 2024, they took a break before setting off on their latest trip - from New Zealand to the UK.
Taking a new pop-top campervan called Trevor, they have reached Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia and they said this was just stage one of their plans, with more trips planned after this one.
The couple plan to visit at least 50 countries over the next six years, travelling through Africa, South America and North America, finishing in Canada.
Their current route has already taken them through New Zealand and Australia and will continue through Malaysia, Thailand, Laos, China, Kurdistan, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Georgia, before arriving in Europe and then back to the UK.
Their last van, Trudy, has been replaced, partly because it was getting old and parts were becoming hard to come by.
But their new vehicle is also cheaper to ship when they have to travel across the sea, because its top can be retracted.
The couple said shipping the larger Trudy was expensive and cost them £8,000 on one journey from Malaysia to India.
Trevor was picked up in March and Chris said it has also been responsible for a few dramas after developing a leaky roof.
That had to be replaced in New Zealand.
On their latest trip they have taken the time to visit Thailand, where they had their honeymoon, 27 years ago.
There, they met a man who they had stayed with on their first visit.
Marianne said: "We rocked up and they called him to come down to the resort and he literally saw us and just cried.
"He still remembered us from, well, nearly 30 years ago."
Reflecting on their travels so far, Marianne said the worst roads had been in India, while the best food had been in Turkey.
"I love the whole Mediterranean thing," she said, while Chris said he had preferred the food in Malaysia.
The couple said their favourite scenery had been in New Zealand and Canada.
"I've got to say they are two epic places for views," Marianne said.
But her favourite moment came in Africa, where they met a mother elephant and her baby.
"I still cry when I think of that moment," Marianne said.
"When the mummy elephant came along and I literally reversed Judy a little bit to give her a bit more space and a baby came out... lifted his trunk up and like squealed.
"She looked at me and she nodded and I'm so grateful that Chris caught it on camera to be able to share it because it was just epic."
With a long way yet to travel, Marianne said: "People say to us all the time, 'oh, the world's so small.'
"I laugh and say, not if you're driving this, because it's thousands of miles."
They have not forgotten their first van, Trudy though.
While Trevor was shipping from Auckland to Sydney, they "dipped home to see family in Shropshire" and while they were there, they got to take Trudy out for another spin.
Marianne said: "We had an epic time and realised everything we loved and missed about her."

articles.title_orig: How a laboratory accident revealed a new way to rescue dying corals
articles.title_zh: How a laboratory accident revealed a new way to rescue dying corals
articles.content_orig:
Dying corals may have found an unexpected lifeline: their neighbours.
Scientists at Stanford University have discovered a way to bring corals back from the brink of death by placing them in contact with healthy corals for just a few days.
Published in Science Advances, the study presents a promising new approach to restoring coral reefs as rising sea temperatures cause more frequent and severe coral bleaching events.
When water becomes too hot, corals expel the microscopic algae that provide much of their energy, an event known as bleaching, which leaves them vulnerable to starvation.
After bleaching events, it can take months or years for surviving corals to recover – but the scientists contend hope is not lost for them.
“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” says lead author Danny Collins, a PhD student at Stanford. “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”
The discovery happened by accident in 2025, when Steve Palumbi, a professor of oceans and marine biologist at Stanford’s Doerr School of Sustainability, noticed two pieces of coral that had fallen against each other in a laboratory tank. One was healthy while the other was bleached. But where the two touched, the bleached coral was beginning to regain its colour.
Collins then arranged 10 pairs of coral fragments, each containing a healthy and bleached piece from the same colony. Five pairs were placed in contact with one another, and the others were kept a few millimetres apart.
Within seven weeks, all five bleached fragments put in contact with their healthy clones had recovered. The ones that were kept apart had died.
Under a microscope, the scientists discovered the corals had fused together, creating tiny channels that allowed algae and nutrients to pass from one to the other. Within three days, beneficial algae had begun moving from the healthy corals into the bleached ones. After about a week, some had received enough algae to recover on their own.
Once inside the damaged corals, the beneficial algae began multiplying rapidly. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals,” says Palumbi.
During the second week, the algae doubled in number every four days – about 10 times faster than in wild corals – allowing the damaged corals to continue recovering even after they were separated from the healthy ones.
The finding marked a breakthrough in the lab. “Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a Stanford professor and one of Collins’ faculty advisors.
But the scientists say the technique isn’t ready for wide-scale application in the oceans .
The corals must be genetically identical for their tissues to fuse. In other words, every damaged coral would need a healthy copy of itself – an impractical solution for restoring whole reefs. But the researchers hope to find ways to deliver the beneficial algae without requiring direct contact or identical twins.
The revelation comes at a crucial time for coral reefs.
According to the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network’s latest assessment, the world's reefs have lost nearly 10 per cent of their living coral over the past four decades. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, it fell almost 9 per cent during a global bleaching event – the largest single-year decline ever recorded.
Global bleaching now occurs roughly every five to six years, leaving reefs less time to recover between bouts of extreme heat. The report warns that reefs will continue declining unless man-made emissions fall and threats such as overfishing, water pollution and coastal developments are curbed.
And while combining coral to help them recover from bleaching might save some of them, Palumbi stresses that it can’t protect them from rising sea temperatures.
“This is a recovery story. It doesn’t blunt heatwaves; it just helps the aftermath. There is still a huge need to reduce heatwaves and protect all of Earth’s life from rapid climate stress,” he says.
“Eventually, it can hopefully help the huge effort being put into restoration succeed better by helping those coral gardens survive heatwaves more completely.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.
