articles.title_orig: Trump administration seeks to strip Ilhan Omar of US citizenship: WSJ
articles.title_zh: Trump administration seeks to strip Ilhan Omar of US citizenship: WSJ
articles.content_orig:
The administration of US President Donald Trump is investigating Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to revoke her citizenship and eventually deport her, The Wall Street Journal has reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the investigation.
The inquiry centres partly on how the Minnesota representative obtained citizenship after arriving in the US as a refugee from Somalia, the newspaper reported on Wednesday. Authorities are examining her family’s immigration records and have issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, seeking testimony before a grand jury in Minnesota.
Omar’s office rejected the investigation as baseless in remarks to the Journal.
The Journal’s report comes just days after US federal agents raided the congresswoman’s home in what her office described as an “unprecedented escalation” by the Trump administration against its political opponents.
The search came just weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, a crucial vote for Republicans vying to retain control of Congress. Omar is seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota’s 5th congressional district.
The Department of Homeland Security said the raid was part of “an ongoing federal investigation”.
Agents took Omar’s passport, mobile phone, personal computers and notebooks, according to people familiar with the search, the newspaper said.
Omar arrived in the US in 1995 after living in a refugee camp in Kenya and became a citizen in 2000. She has previously denied committing immigration fraud.
At issue in the citizenship inquiry is whether Omar or her late father altered her age in immigration paperwork to indicate that she was 17 rather than 18 when her father applied for citizenship, the Journal reported.
According to the newspaper, investigators are examining whether that allowed her to acquire citizenship through her father rather than having to undergo a separate application process.
Omar’s father died in 2020, complicating efforts to collect evidence on whether Omar lied about her own age – which, according to a former top immigration official in the Justice Department, the Trump administration would hinge its case on – or whether her father lied on her behalf.
The Journal also reported that Homeland Security Investigations officials examined a similar allegation during the administration of former President Joe Biden but did not pursue it because they lacked evidence of fraud.
The newspaper did not report that anyone had filed a lawsuit seeking to revoke Omar’s citizenship. Such a case would require court proceedings, as the investigation itself does not revoke her citizenship or authorise her deportation.
The newspaper reported that a nonpartisan congressional watchdog had earlier cleared Omar of wrongdoing over disclosures that overstated her assets.
Agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), searched Omar’s home under what the department called a “judicially authorized search warrant”.
On Monday morning, agents blocked off the street around Omar’s home and removed boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”.
Omar, a prominent progressive Democrat, has faced years of attacks from Trump and his allies over her Somali background and immigration history.
Hours after the Monday raid, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with the search, saying it was “really up to the DOJ [Justice Department]”.

articles.title_orig: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.title_zh: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.content_orig:
The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."
She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.
Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.
In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

articles.title_zh: Ancient Chinese parents gave babies nicknames – ‘Dog’, ‘Pig’ – to protect them
articles.content_orig:
Some believe these humble nicknames carry parents’ heartfelt blessings and should be preserved
Like people elsewhere in the world, Chinese people often have nicknames in addition to their official names. Some of these may surprise people from other cultures because they sound humble or even unflattering.
Chinese parents have traditionally given their children humble, sometimes vulgar, nicknames – occasionally using animal names such as “Dog” or “Pig.” The practice dates back to ancient times.
Parents believed that the humbler a nickname sounded, the better, as it might help ensure their child grew up healthy.
This practice was a desperate measure in ancient times, when medical technology was limited and people’s average lifespans were short.

articles.title_orig: U.S. warnings sow confusion, alarm in Ukraine over intelligence, Starlink access
articles.title_zh: U.S. warnings sow confusion, alarm in Ukraine over intelligence, Starlink access
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Hastings Introduces Regional Demonstrators Program
articles.title_zh: Hastings Introduces Regional Demonstrators Program
articles.content_orig:
Hastings Fiber Glass Products has expanded its Demonstrator program and introduced regional Demonstrators to provide better, dedicated coverage of the United States hot line tools and equipment market.
By adding three new Demonstrators and subject matter experts to its team, the program staff now possesses a combined 95 years of field experience using hot line tools and equipment.
In addition to long-time Hastings ’ team member John Giancanelli, the Demonstrator team now includes Ben Hoover, Colby Quaife and Ryon Roberts.
As a Demonstrator, each team member uses first-hand industry knowledge to show proper tool use and capabilities, provide safety and compliance instruction, manage client relationships and relay feedback to engineering for product innovation and improvements.
“Expanding our Demonstrator presence with people who know the job and the tools is important for Hastings Fiber Glass Products,” said Brian Baum, CEO of Hastings . “Having people who have worked in the field, know the risks first-hand and can share practical, real-world solutions helps keep end users of Hastings ’ products safe and supported on the job.
“John has been the foundation of our educational efforts for nearly two decades,” Baum said. “Adding Ben, Colby, and Ryon to the team will help expand upon his expertise and coverage area.”
Before joining Hastings in 2008, Giancanelli worked as a lineworker, first responder, and lead in the field for 20 years. He relocated from Hastings ’ headquarters in Michigan to Texas, allowing him to focus on the central United States, including North Dakota and Minnesota, south to Texas. He shares Arkansas and Louisiana with Quaife and Roberts, and Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico with Hoover.
“I’ve restored power due to earthquakes, riots, fires, floods, avalanches and various storms,” Giancanelli said. “I can’t think of much I didn’t do in line work from 115 kV down, and I’m thankful for the experience.”
In his role at Hastings , he enjoys having face-to-face conversations and being able to provide answers and solutions in real time.
“The customers know we’ve traveled to see them, which is important, especially if they have a problem,” he added. “Listening to them and then providing a qualified, satisfying solution is rewarding.”
As a new addition to the team, Hoover, who is based in Colorado, covers the West Coast and eastward as far as Montana, Idaho, Utah, and Arizona. He shares Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico with Giancanelli.
With 20 years in energy distribution, Hoover has worked as a journeyman lineman, lead and foreman.
“I used Hastings ’ products for my whole line career,” Hoover said, “So I know they make good products and stand by them.”
Finding ways to make the trade easier and safer is Hoover’s favorite part of being a Demonstrator.
Quaife, a former Marine based in Florida, joins Hastings with 20 years of journeyman lineman experience in transmission hot sticking and live line barehand and distribution, as well as 2 ½ years as a tool demonstrator elsewhere. He serves the East Coast, including states East of the Mississippi River, along with Hoover.
“As a Demonstrator, I get to travel around, work with customers and put our tools in people's hands so they can see them in action,” Quaife said. “I enjoy talking with customers, hearing about the work they do, and helping them find solutions that make their jobs easier.
“The best part of the job is meeting people from all over and being able to represent a company and products I believe in,” he added.
Roberts, also new to Hastings , is based in Florida and covers the East Coast, including states East of the Mississippi River, along with Quaife. He has 35 years of experience in energy distribution and as a first responder for transmission, including serving as a journeyman lineman, line trainer, lead line trainer, supervisor and manager.
He enjoys traveling the East Coast and beyond to share Hastings ’ products and suggest techniques for their use, care and maintenance. Solving problems experienced in the field is the most rewarding part of his role as a Hastings Demonstrator.
In addition to the regions and states specified for each Demonstrator, Alaska and Hawaii are covered by availability within the team.

articles.title_orig: Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
articles.title_zh: Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has suggested that those who leak information to the news media should be shot as punishment.
Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, as he urged supporters to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.
“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump told the crowd. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
Trump made the statement in an apparent reference to Operation Midnight Hammer, which saw the US launch a surprise attack on Iran in June 2025 during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran.
In the aftermath of the attack, several media outlets published findings from a preliminary report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency.
That report – which had not yet been released to the public – indicated that Iran was able to move some of its enriched uranium away from the sites the US had bombed.
It also suggested that the extent of the damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities was more modest than what Trump had asserted.
Trump, however, appeared to signal that the timing of the US attacks was among the leaked information. He accused the news media of putting military members in danger, calling out The New York Times and CNN in particular.
“They leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving,” Trump said, claiming he had to reschedule the bombing campaign two days later as a result.
“Somebody leaked. Some sleaze-bag, they ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail.”
Trump has long had an adversarial relationship with the news media, and he has previously called for harsh punishment against any official who passes on confidential information to news outlets.
After parts of the Defense Intelligence Agency report became public, he blamed lawmakers in the Democratic Party for its release.
“The Democrats are the ones who leaked the information on the PERFECT FLIGHT to the Nuclear Sites in Iran,” Trump wrote on social media at the time. “They should be prosecuted!”
Under Trump, the White House has taken aggressive action to track down the source of leaks.
Staff in his administration , as well as officers in the military, have also been asked to take polygraph tests.
Journalists at several news outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal, have also received subpoenas aimed at determining the sources of internal information made public.
The newspapers had reported on stories such as a botched Navy SEALs raid in North Korea and how Trump ignored internal Pentagon warnings against launching the Iran war.
Last year, the Department of Defense demanded that journalists who wished to access the Pentagon sign an agreement not to publish unauthorised material.
Much of the Pentagon press corps refused to agree, and a federal court struck down many of the new demands made on journalists at the department.
Trump has long raged against leakers, going back to his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.
Former White House official Alyssa Farah Griffin told a podcast in 2024 that Trump had called for leakers to be executed, after media outlets reported that he had taken shelter in a White House bunker during racial justice protests in 2020.
Trump appeared to reprise that sentiment in his speech to Arizona voters on Wednesday, less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.
“Leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump said. “To me, they are the scum of the earth.”

articles.title_orig: Global tech sell-off deepens as Asian markets tumble
articles.title_zh: Global tech sell-off deepens as Asian markets tumble
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A global sell-off in memory-chip stocks deepened overnight as South Korea's benchmark KOSPI ( ^KS11 ) tanked 7%.
Micron ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) were poised to open lower on Wednesday as SK Hynix ( 000660.KS ) and Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) fell 10% and 8%, respectively, after tanking earlier this week over concerns about intensifying competition from China. The two memory giants account for more than half of the South Korean stock market's total capitalization.
The sell-off in South Korea followed a decline in the chip sector on Wall Street on Wednesday as worries about further rate hikes collided with fears of AI-driven debt financing.
Chip giant Nvidia ( NVDA ), Broadcom ( AVGO ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) all led the chip stocks lower during the session.
On Wednesday, worries about borrowing costs also hit the AI trade.
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock fell more than 15% after a chart of the neocloud providers' bond yields circulated on social media.
The stock's sharp sell-off highlighted concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale fast enough to manage its growing interest expense.
Any slowdown in AI spending could spell trouble for chip makers, which have been the main beneficiaries of infrastructure spending as hyperscalers race to build out data centers.
On Thursday, investors will get another glimpse of the health of the AI buildout when TSMC ( TSM ) reports quarterly results. Investors expect quarterly profits to rise 60%.
Investors will pay close attention to the foundry's capacity, given ASML's ( ASML ) results on Wednesday. The maker of advanced chip-making machines warned it may not be able to fully meet demand in 2027 and 2008.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Sally Rooney’s publisher pulls books from UK over her support for outlawed anti-Israel group
articles.title_zh: Sally Rooney’s publisher pulls books from UK over her support for outlawed anti-Israel group
articles.content_orig:
The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK, makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws
I t’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacle with her eyes open: she said last July that royalties from her books, and their BBC adaptations, would be used to support Palestine Action .
Rooney’s courage is not so much in risking imprisonment , since there is a fix for that, which is what she’s doing – avoiding the UK. Rather, she has chosen the thorniest possible path for this cause. Authors can write essays and sign letters in support of the Palestinian people; actors can voice it in interviews, musicians can say it from the stage, and there is always a cost to it, whether it’s in plain sight and they’ve been kicked off a global tour, or it’s behind closed doors and they are simply excluded from opportunities. But such actions, even if they logically suggest support for a proscribed organisation, don’t entail actively breaking the terrorism laws. Rooney had taken a financial hit anyway, by pledging support for Palestine Action with her royalties; but that’s a price at least you can count. The lost sales and opportunities that ripple out from being effectively both barred from and banned in the UK are innumerable.
Yet, speaking as not-her-accountant, but as someone living in the culture she also inhabits and has made such an impact describing, the value of her stand is similarly hard to put a price on. Her authorial voice and body of work makes this intervention distinctive in its reach. She’s never been an apolitical author. Normal People was razor sharp on class, Conversations With Friends wasn’t shy of a Marxist analysis. But the work is also intimate, often domestic, I mean, the clue’s in the name – these were always normal people. It was from a reputation of delicately challenging but everyday subtlety that Rooney assumed her outrider position, and in so doing, took on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choice; insisted that it is a human response, as natural and quotidian, as passionate and important, as friendship.
It also, come on – surely at some point we’re allowed to say this – makes an absolute mockery of the terrorism legislation thus applied. Nobody anywhere thinks Sally Rooney poses a danger to the British state, or any state, just as nobody anywhere thinks a 94-year-old human rights barrister who was a friend of Ed Miliband’s late mother does. Keir Starmer, paradoxically, given that the two things in his favour were his caution and his legal hinterland, painted himself into an absurd corner, where terrorism arrests went up between 2024 and 2025 from 250 to nearly 3,000 . On demos where anyone crunched the numbers, more of them were over 80 than under 20 .
The history and particularity of Irish solidarity with the Palestinian cause have been discussed a lot since the painful Ed Sheeran tour, in which the singer thought a support act could be quietly ditched over a pro-Palestine song, without losing his backing band – Beoga , founder members of Irish Artists for Palestine. More broadly, Ireland has a vibrant tradition of young women with no reason to think they have the right to opine on geopolitics sticking their oar in anyway. The Dunnes Stores strike of 1984 kicked off when 21-year-old Mary Manning refused to handle some South African grapefruit, leading to her receiving only £21 a week in strike pay for two years and nine months. It reached its political crescendo less than three years later, when Ireland banned South African goods altogether in protest at apartheid. In between, though, in 1985, Desmond Tutu met Manning and her fellow strikers on his way to get the Nobel peace prize, extending as he did an invitation to visit him in South Africa – which they took him up on, only to be turned away at the border. There’s an instant echo, here, of a state showing its might at customs only to draw attention to its weakness; and of an author who, as well as that, is an ordinary citizen, whose forgone royalties are almost the least of the sacrifice, but are still a powerful emblem.

articles.content_orig:

Nepal and the World Bank Group Announce Partnership to Explore Catastrophe Bond for Earthquake Risk
https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/statement/2026/10/15/nepal-and-the-world-bank-group-announce-partnership-to-explore-catastrophe-bond-fo
BANGKOK, October 15, 2026 — Nepal and the World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, IBRD, Aaa/AAA) signed a mandate agreement to explore the development of a catastrophe bond to help Nepal access funds quickly in case of a major earthquake.
The agreement marks the beginning of a collaboration to assess how capital markets can support Nepal's broader disaster risk management strategy. As one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, Nepal is working to better prepare for, withstand, and recover from future natural disasters through a combination of risk reduction, preparedness, and financial protection measures.
Under the agreement, the World Bank Group Treasury will work with the Government of Nepal and market participants to assess the feasibility and potential structure of such a transaction.
This initiative is part of the World Bank Group’s established catastrophe bond program, which has helped countries access international capital markets to transfer disaster risk and secure financial protection against natural hazards. More information on the program is available on the World Bank Group Treasury website: World Bank Group Catastrophe Bond Program.
Kathmandu: Akash Shrestha, ashrestha9@worldbank.org

articles.title_orig: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco’s headquarters, officials say
articles.title_zh: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco’s headquarters, officials say
articles.content_orig:
A building owned by the energy giant Aramco was set ablaze late Tuesday in a strike on the Saudi city housing its headquarters, the kingdom’s energy ministry said, as war spiked between the Houthi militia in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis had threatened earlier in the day to attack the Aramco headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran, but did not immediately take responsibility for the strike. It came after the Iranian-backed militia reported that two major oil facilities in Yemen had been attacked by Saudi forces on Tuesday.
The Saudi energy ministry said in a statement that the strike in Dhahran had hit an Aramco administrative building and caused “a limited fire” and no injuries.
By late Tuesday, residents of both countries were on edge as explosions were repeatedly heard in their capital cities. A Saudi-led coalition said it was targeting Yemeni facilities that support the Houthi war effort, while the Houthis vowed to retaliate against comparable sites in Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi authorities issued warnings of an aerial threat in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. And Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said four cruise missiles fired toward Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia had been intercepted, along with two drones.
Mr. al-Maliki also reported that a ballistic missile launched toward the city of Damman in the eastern part of the kingdom by the Houthis had been intercepted, and that shrapnel fell in a residential area of neighboring Dhahran.

articles.title_orig: A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria
articles.title_zh: A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria
articles.content_orig:
According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000.
The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000.
Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible.
Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.
Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.
In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.
Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines .
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.

articles.title_orig: Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
articles.title_zh: Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
articles.content_orig:
Badakhshan Province, 4 October 2026, covering the Wakhan Corridor and Pamir region in Afghanistan (Javid Ashna via Getty Images)
In treacherous terrain, the Taliban has carved a path to potentially strengthen its position with China and against Pakistan.
Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.
You may unsubscribe from Lowy Institute newsletters at any time. For information on our privacy practices and how to unsubscribe, see our Privacy Policy .
Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
The Taliban regime in Afghanistan has spent 365 million Afghanis – about US$5.5 million – building a road through one of the most remote corners of the country towards the Chinese border. It may turn out to be little more than a rough mountain road. But it could also give Afghanistan something it lacks: leverage.
At the northeastern edge of Afghanistan in the Wakhan Corridor, (Opens in new window) this new road is quietly changing the strategic geography. The Taliban's Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development inaugurated (Opens in new window) the 121-kilometre gravel road on 4 October 2026, running from Broghil in Wakhan district to China’s border. The route includes four bridges, 66 culverts and more than 3,000 metres of retaining walls.
The road does not yet mean that Afghan trucks can simply drive into China, and there is no commercial border crossing. But it brings Afghanistan physically closer to a country that has become increasingly important to the Taliban's regional diplomacy. That possibility matters.
For years, Afghanistan has depended heavily on Pakistan for access to international markets. That dependence has become uncomfortable as relations between Kabul and Islamabad have deteriorated. The two countries shut major border crossings after deadly fighting in October 2025, disrupting bilateral trade and leaving hundreds of trucks stranded. The closure exposed how vulnerable Afghanistan remains to decisions made by its neighbour.
The consequences have gone beyond trade and impacts citizens. Before the closure, more than 70% (Opens in new window) of medicines used in Afghanistan were imported from Pakistan, according to the European Union Agency for Asylum. So, the attraction of another route is obvious.
The Wakhan Corridor is a narrow strip of Afghan territory extending eastwards between Tajikistan and Pakistan before reaching China's Xinjiang region. Its strategic importance is hardly new (Opens in new window) . During the 19th century’s Great Game era, it served as a buffer between the British Empire in India and the Russian Empire to the north.
The mountains that once made Wakhan useful as a buffer also made it extraordinarily difficult to reach. High passes, severe winters and poor infrastructure have kept the corridor isolated. The new road does not change that geography, but it does begin to work around it, and Beijing has been paying attention.
In February, Afghanistan's ambassador to China, Mawlawi Asadullah Bilal Karimi, met Liu Jinsong, head of the Department of Asian Affairs at China's foreign ministry. According to Chinese and Afghan accounts, the discussions included China-Afghanistan relations. Afghan reporting also said activation of the Wakhan Corridor was discussed.
In March, Afghanistan’s Acting Minister of Commerce Nooruddin Azizi also met China's Special Representative in Kabul, Yu Xiaoyong (Opens in new window) in Kabul to discuss connectivity and transit.
While this demonstrates diplomacy around the idea, there is a distinction between a road reaching China, and China agreeing to open a full commercial crossing. Beijing has made no public commitment to do so, and that is likely to remain the challenge.
A functioning trade route would require customs facilities, security arrangements and infrastructure, as well as a road capable of handling sustained commercial traffic. A high-altitude gravel road through the Pamirs is a different proposition from a modern trade corridor.
China's calculations are likely to be cautious for another reason: security. (Opens in new window) Beijing has maintained pragmatic relations with the Taliban while stressing its concerns about militant groups operating from Afghan territory, particularly those that could threaten China's Xinjiang region. China has also supported security cooperation along the Wakhan frontier. In 2025, China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi (Opens in new window) said Beijing supported the resumption of bilateral patrols in the corridor and called for stronger Afghan action against the East Turkestan Islamic Movement and other militant groups.
For Beijing, therefore, the road is not simply about moving goods. It is also about what happens in the mountains beside Xinjiang. This is where the road becomes more interesting than its modest size suggests.
The new road does not change that geography, but it does begin to work around it, and Beijing has been paying attention.
Afghanistan has long been described as a potential bridge between Central Asia, China, South Asia and the Middle East. Its geography offers that possibility, but decades of war, political instability and inadequate infrastructure have prevented it from becoming reality. The Taliban now appears determined to test that proposition. (Opens in new window)
The most ambitious possibility would be a wider network linking China through Afghanistan to Iran and the Arabian Sea. Afghanistan already has access to Iran's Chabahar port, which offers an alternative to Pakistan's seaports. But that route has also been subject to geopolitical uncertainty, making the search for multiple routes more significant. But it would be a mistake to portray the Wakhan road as a ready-made alternative to Pakistan's ports, as the road is only the first piece of a larger puzzle.
Beijing may see value in greater economic access to Afghanistan. It may also see strategic value in having another potential connection to Central Asia and the wider region. But China has shown little appetite for taking unnecessary risks in Afghanistan. The road therefore matters less because it guarantees trade than because it creates possibility.
For Kabul, the symbolism is powerful. The Taliban can point to a domestically funded infrastructure project reaching towards China at a time when Afghanistan remains internationally isolated. More practically, it gives Kabul a card to play in its difficult relationship with Pakistan.
Shadi Khan Saif is a Melbourne-based journalist and a former Afghanistan/Pakistan correspondent for Reuters and Deutsche Welle.

articles.title_orig: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.title_zh: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.content_orig:
Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online
A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago , as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.
The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.
In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.
She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.
A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.
The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.
No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.
Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.
“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.
“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”
The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.
Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.
Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

articles.title_orig: SC US Senate campaign escalates on China, law enforcement
articles.title_zh: SC US Senate campaign escalates on China, law enforcement
articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday, the war of words ramped up across the Palmetto State between U.S. Senate candidates, Republican Sen. Darline Graham and her Democratic challenger, Dr. Annie Andrews.
The candidates held dueling events in the Lowcountry and Upstate, as they look to get any edge with undecided voters in a race recent polls show is a close contest.
The increasingly heated campaign rhetoric and back-and-forth tied to China, foreign policy, and law enforcement comes less than a week before the start of early voting and less than three weeks until Election Day.
“National security isn’t an elective in this job," Andrews said during an event Wednesday morning in Charleston. There, she cited a recent Washington Post report that claimed Graham's husband is an executive at a company connected to Chinese weapons manufacturing.
Andrews said that the senator's family should cut any business ties to China and that Graham should recuse herself from any votes involving trade with China or Chinese military policy.
“I think it’s just important that we always put America first, American interests first, American security interests, privacy interests, data security interests, first and foremost," Andrews said. "To me, it’s a non-story; I mean, she’s desperate obviously," Graham said, who responded to Andrews' claims at an event Wednesday afternoon in Spartanburg — and pushed back on the claims in the Washington Post article.
"Bringing my husband into this is absolutely wrong; he’s an employee at a company," Graham said. "He doesn’t own it, he doesn’t have any shares in the company, he’s never been to China, he doesn’t make decisions like that, so I think it’s completely unfair to my husband.” On Wednesday afternoon in Greenville, several sheriffs of Upstate counties also officially endorsed Graham, citing her commitment to law enforcement funding.
“We understand her support for law enforcement," Greenville County Sheriff Hobart Lewis said.
In response, an Andrews campaign spokesperson said Graham failed to sign on to legislation that would help police officers buy homes and strengthen collective bargaining protections.
